📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it might sound a bit vapid to us in the hoi polloi, but even those who can afford super-rare, super-low-volume production supercars still want to stand out from their peers. As a result, plenty of design houses offer aftermarket body kits and tuning for supercars and super-SUVs, but more often than not, they look somewhat ... atrocious. Novitec, however, is firmly bucking that trend with a upcoming subtle upgrade for the Ferrari 12Cilindri—and it leveraged a classic designer to help pull it off.

It has been revealed that that designer is Vittorio Strosek, a man who has played a role in classic reimaginings of cars from Lamborghini, Porsche, McLaren, Bugatti, and more. Now, he's collaborating with Novitec to put a latest face on the 12Cilindri. The result is a car that looks noticeably different than the original, without losing much of what makes that Ferrari so desirable.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced version picks up a new front bumper, new hood, new side panels, new rear arches, and a new rear fascia. Sure, it's clearly still a 12Cilindri, but it's also clearly different when set side by side with the version that rolls out of the factory gates; the Novitec car ends up being 2.8 inches wider at the front and 5.1 inches wider at the rear. The hood outlet exposes the red intake manifolds, and the entire package allegedly reduces front lift and improves rear downforce. Novitec also added Vossen wheels measuring 21 inches up front and 22 inches in the back.

It has been revealed that let's break down a few of the finer details here. Perhaps most obviously, the black panel at the front of the car is long gone. Instead, the section matches the body color. Then, on the fenders, you'll find fresh vents that help to evacuate air that could otherwise be trapped in the wheel wells. The deep V cutouts on the hood are gone, in favor of a singular intake in the middle.

According to recent reports, the side of the car is also dramatically different. There are vents and intakes at the front and rear, where the normal car has neither; then, at the very back, the rear window is gone in favor of louvers. The sections that are black in the normal car also end up with panels that match the body. (I’d say the ducktail spoiler looks good too.) Overall, it's a cohesive design that manages to stand out without being overtly gaudy. As aftermarket supercar body kits go, this is one of the better ones out there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

Industry observers note that when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

In a recent development, power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Recent findings suggest that why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the newly introduced NX7 in the comments, today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

Industry observers note that by 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

It has been revealed that the researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

It has been revealed that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

Recent findings suggest that however, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she noted.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

It has been revealed that more than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” mentioned Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick noted.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

It has been revealed that “Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an key factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

Industry observers note that from sweaty runs and heat styling to product buildup, our scalps and hair need proper TLC—and that starts with a great shampoo. Our scalp is an extension of the skin on our face—it sheds dead skin cells, collects dirt and bacteria, and secretes oil and sweat, claims trichologist Anabel Kingsley in our guide on how often to shampoo your hair. While the beauty community has mixed opinions on the cadence of shampooing, dermatologist DiAnne Davis, MD, recommends doing so at least once a week. The frequency varies based on your lifestyle, how quickly your hair gets greasy, your scalp health, and hair type. Since the experts advise regular shampooing, I asked the pros about how we can upgrade our healthy hair routines to preserve the expensive chemical and color treatments we enjoy at the salon.

“I always tell my clients that shampoo is mainly for your scalp, so I would start there,” says trichologist and hairstylist Courtney Foster. “You can have curly hair with an oily scalp, fine hair with a dry scalp, or color-treated hair with buildup. Hair type matters, but it doesn't tell me everything I need to know.” Choose hydrating shampoos that nourish a dry scalp, or use a lightweight shampoo with fewer moisturizing ingredients for an oily scalp.

Sources indicate that for an oily scalp or buildup, ingredients like salicylic acid can be helpful, along with gentle cleansing agents like coco glucoside. For mineral and hard water buildup, look for chelating ingredients, as regular shampoo alone may not remove these deposits, according to Foster.

Now it’s time to think about your hair type, advises Foster. In addition to your hair texture, you’ll want to find a shampoo that’s suitable for your dry, chemically treated, damaged, or breakage-prone mane.

For dryness, humectants and conditioning ingredients such as glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and nourishing oils are your new beauty best friends. They help the hair retain moisture and feel softer and more manageable, notes Foster.

For damaged hair, you’ll need shampoos packed with amino acids and bond-strengthening ingredients. “These are good for hair that has been chemically treated or excessively heat-styled,” she says of components such as hydrolyzed proteins, which can improve the feel and strength of damaged hair.

Now, if you’re dealing with frizz like I am, it likely means the hair is lacking moisture, claims Foster. We’ll benefit from conditioning ingredients like polymers, silicones, oils, and humectants that help smooth the cuticle and improve manageability.

Sources indicate that as our hair-obsessed beauty editor, I own a sizable shampoo collection. It’s 24 shampoos strong. So I started there and narrowed it down to 12 contenders. In addition to expert guidance—ingredients for a healthy scalp and cosmetic concerns like frizz—I factored in everything from their cleansing power, lather, fragrance, and feel. Did they leave my scalp parched like I just went swimming in the pool? Or did they help rebalance my scalp and prevent embarrassing flakes on my black clothing?

To help whittle down potential recommendations even further, I recruited the Women’s Health team, including beauty director Brian Underwood and deputy editor Carina Hsieh, to test these picks. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight.
  • Industry observers note that the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

Industry observers note that the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

Sources indicate that the CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

In a recent development, the program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

In a recent development, the obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL introduced its aviation unit.

Industry observers note that CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and remarked it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither manufacturer has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, Latest York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

Recent findings suggest that for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

According to recent reports, and this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

It has been revealed that if you’re following the electrification of transport, the cheapest place to start is your own roof: home solar can power your EV for close to nothing. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #64032. Tech Report: When We Forgive, What New Meaning Do We Find in Life?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1244 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: When We Forgive, What New Meaning Do We Find in Life?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • Recent findings suggest that suffering could lead to despair, depression, hopelessness, and even not liking oneself (Yu et al.
  • The psychotherapist and Holocaust survivor, Viktor Frankl (1969/2014), pioneered this idea of finding meaning in suffering as he endured the persecution of his imprisonment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Recent findings suggest that suffering could lead to despair, depression, hopelessness, and even not liking oneself (Yu et al. 2021; Reed & Enright, 2006). Yet one aspect of the forgiveness process, especially as one nears the end of the forgiveness journey, is the sometimes surprising development of finding meaning in that suffering and a fresh purpose in life. Finding meaning centers on an important question: What have I learned from going through this suffering, and what have I learned as I walked the journey of forgiveness? This is a cognitive exercise that can lead to new short-term and long-term goals (Enright, 2015). In other words, the cognitive exercise of finding meaning can lead to behaviors that support new purposes in one’s life.

The psychotherapist and Holocaust survivor, Viktor Frankl (1969/2014), pioneered this idea of finding meaning in suffering as he endured the persecution of his imprisonment. His motivation was to resist being destroyed by the abuse. By finding meaning, one can transcend suffering and make it more bearable.

In a recent development, when I discuss the theme of finding meaning in suffering through forgiveness, I am not focusing on the injustice but on its aftermath. The basic question is this: What are you learning about life as you extend mercy to those who were deeply unfair to you? This post explores the different meanings people tend to generate as they forgive.

Let us first start by examining what finding meaning in suffering is not, because it can be misunderstood.

Consider three themes that sometimes are confused with finding meaning in what an unjustly acting person has done to the forgiver.

Sources indicate that first, the forgiver is not denying the disappointment, sadness, anger, or grief in what was suffered. The injustice did happen, and the negative response is real. In other words, finding meaning is not some kind of non-feeling, interpreted, at least temporarily, as relief from the effects of the injustice.

Industry observers note that second, the person does not play games with themselves, stating, for example, “Oh well, things happen for a reason, and I’ll just make the best of it by accepting it.” Yes, people can “make the best of it,” but if this is an exclusive meaning of suffering, the one who forgives is not going after the woundedness inside, which may linger for a long time. The “oh well” approach is passive. To heal from the effects of the injustice, a person needs a more active approach to the pain.

It has been revealed that third, the forgiver does not distort reality by thinking, “Well, all things happen for good reasons, and so I will try to see the good in what happened to me.” The injustice was not good. Some aspects of what happens after the injustice may be good, but the injustice itself is not.

Consider six points on this question.

Industry observers note that 1. Being more sensitive to the suffering of others, even those who never hurt you: James, upon forgiving, realized he had what he called a “short temper,” in which he imposed his anger on unsuspecting others. He has now committed, for example, to being more patient and kind to cashiers in grocery stores and pharmacies as he waits in line. He is more sensitive to the fatigue and stress of those working behind the cash register. This gives him a new sense of purpose, as he recognizes his intemperance in these contexts and now works to overcome his anger.

Industry observers note that 2. Being motivated to help others in their suffering: When Dr. Freedman (Freedman & Enright, 1996) worked with female incest survivors on a long-term forgiveness intervention, she saw that many of them, upon forgiving, became motivated to help other incest survivors overcome their deep resentment. They were not choosing as a goal to become mental health professionals, but instead to be of assistance to others who have suffered as they have.

In a recent development, as another example, I talked with a man who is imprisoned for life. Upon forgiving those who abused him, he stated to me that he knows he will never get out of the correctional institution, but now he is motivated to help his cellmates forgive and to be unburdened of their anger. This led to a upcoming purpose, or the behavioral manifestation of this desire to assist others.

3. Standing in the pain so you do not throw that pain onto others: The paradox of standing in the pain is this: As people bear the negative effects of unjust treatment by not throwing that pain back to the offending person or to unsuspecting others, the pain-bearers realize they are stronger than they thought. They see the positive outcomes of not seeking revenge. As Gandhi remarked, if we keep taking an eye for an eye, the whole world will be blind. The pain-bearers realize they can now translate this into a upcoming purpose of contributing to a more peaceful world.

4. Forgiving helps us think more deeply about justice: If people are continually treated unjustly, they can find meaning in living a life of mercy and fairness integrated together. Thus, their understanding of justice can become wiser, and therefore their appropriation of justice can become more helpful to others.

5. Eventually, you can develop an overall philosophy of life, such as committing to be a conduit of good in this world: This is what Dr. Frankl called supra-meaning, or a new philosophy of life that encompasses an overall approach to how one interacts with others and why one does so in this way. For example, a person can commit to living a life of greater respect, kindness, and love toward both offenders and others. For example, Sally decided to resist impatience and negative emotions toward her own children, as a way of life in her family, so that these life-giving moral virtues can become norms there.

Industry observers note that 6. As people find meaning in their suffering, they can put their future purpose in life into sharper perspective: Finding meaning, in other words, becomes the cognitive rationale and emotional motivation to seek what matters to them.

In a recent development, in summary, our suffering is not for nothing. People who suffer and forgive can develop as they think carefully about what they are learning about suffering, their own humanity, and life itself. As Dr. Frankl learned and passed his wisdom on to us, finding meaning in suffering opens unexpected doors for survival and growing in our humanity.

According to recent reports, enright, R.D. (2015). 8 keys to forgiveness. Norton.

Frankl, V. (1969/2014). The will to meaning: Foundations and applications of logotherapy. Plume.

Freedman, S. R., & Enright, R. D. (1996). Forgiveness as an intervention goal with incest survivors. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 64(5), 983-992.

According to recent reports, reed, G. & Enright, R.D. (2006). The effects of forgiveness therapy on depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress for women after spousal emotional abuse. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 74, 920-929.

It has been revealed that yu, L., Gambaro, M., Song, J., Teslik, M., Komoski, M.C., Wollner, B., & Enright, R.D. (2021). Forgiveness therapy in a maximum-security correctional institution: A randomized clinical trial. Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy, 28, 1457-1471.

#64031. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

In a recent development, they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

According to recent reports, the authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these upcoming reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah mentioned.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is notable, especially for risk reduction.

She said problems with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg noted.

It has been revealed that suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” mentioned Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

Industry observers note that “These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” mentioned William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

Industry observers note that the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” noted Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

Sources indicate that the organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

Industry observers note that the authors of that report listed several steps they mentioned could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu stated.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She noted that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

It has been revealed that khan noted women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

Sources indicate that “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that texas-based startup (and resurrector of an old name) REO Trucks unveiled its revamped and renewed mission and previewed its first vehicle this past summer, but as of Monday, the American startup has some trucks to show us. Or, at least some renderings of some vehicles, alongside some real illustrations by frankstephenson design.

It has been revealed that all three vehicles REO intends to release are detailed and pictured here. The T4X is the work truck; the T4C is the crew cab pickup; and the S4C is a family SUV. All three ride on the same steel ladder frame, and are even identical in every way from the B-pillar forward. It’s beyond the B-pillar where each, naturally, differ based on their specific use cases.

It has been revealed that the T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed. Said bed measures 79.1 inches long and 70.6 inches wide. The tailgate has some neat features with integrated cup holders, recesses for phones or tablets, and bottle openers on either side.

According to recent reports, the T4C crew cab trades some of the bed length for passenger space, as it seats up to five people. That said, the bed is still fairly long, at 54.1 inches in length.

Meanwhile, the S4C seats six, and notably has a shorter rear overhang than the trucks to help with the departure angle for off-roading. The cargo area can be accessed via a side-hinged tailgate, and the rear glass even drops down into the door.

Industry observers note that these are the unique body style features REO is detailing for now, but they all have much more in common than they do differences. For example, each REO vehicle will be equipped with a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine that the company claims is designed for longevity, drive-ability and towing more than outright performance. A six-speed manual transmission comes standard, while a six-speed automatic gearbox will be optional. Every REO is also fitted with part-time four-wheel drive, allowing you to select 2WD or 4WD High/Low via a floor-mounted lever. A locking rear differential will be optional for those who want it.

Expect a bumpy ride, because in addition to the body-on-frame construction, all REOs will have solid axles front and rear. Disc brakes will be fitted up front, but drums are used in the back. You’ll steer with hydraulic assistance, and 17-inch steel wheels will be wrapped by all-season tires. Should off-roading be in your future, a “Ransom Package” will be optional, adding off-road tires with unique off-road wheels, upgraded dampers/leaf springs, and a 2.5-inch suspension lift. (You’ll also get orange accents that designate it as the Ransom Package model.).

Photos of the interior aren’t available, but REO says physical controls will “take prominence.” Unlike the Slate Truck, power windows come standard, but the seats are manually adjustable. There will still be screens, though, as REO says it comes with a digital cluster and display for navigation and media.

Industry observers note that as of now, the T4X is slated to start at $21,500 and be sold in a direct-sales model (no dealers). The T4C is meant to starts at $25,000, and the S4C at $28,500. The organization claims it aims to assemble all three in Texas. While the T4X is meant to reach buyers in late 2028, neither the crew cab pickup nor the SUV have predicted on-sale dates yet; if you want one, REO is taking refundable $25 deposits.

Industry News: High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the firm won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

In a recent development, “Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the manufacturer has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The significant trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite.
  • According to recent reports, but these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

According to recent reports, but these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Sources indicate that early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, states Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

According to recent reports, other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

It has been revealed that images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” says Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Ahead of looks by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

According to recent reports, “You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” says Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) blueprint to adopt this reusable design.

In a recent development, even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley indicates the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into upcoming materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley indicates that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” indicates Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

It has been revealed that autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie declared the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the organization really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

In a recent development, “We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” notes Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” stated Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The tech giant notes the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially key, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Sources indicate that experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” mentioned Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

  • Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to newly introduced research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

Recent findings suggest that the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, stated Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

Sources indicate that “By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she remarked.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz mentioned the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

In a recent development, she said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

It has been revealed that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

In a recent development, A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

In a recent development, “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy mentioned.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Sources indicate that wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, released in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Recent findings suggest that the study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also remarked the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham noted adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive blueprint,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

Pearley: How the Saab 99 Turbo Changed the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history.
  • Yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America).
  • According to recent reports, the 99 was already ancient by 1977.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history. Commercially, this was the model year when General Motors “downsized” its full-size cars from gargantuan to merely huge. Their immense sales success meant the era of land dreadnoughts was over. It was the first model year for the BMW 3-Series name in America and the first for the Porsche 924, that company’s first front-engine car. In Formula One, Colin Chapman introduced ground effects aerodynamics to the series with the revolutionary Lotus 78. Culturally, 1977 was the year of Smokey and the Bandit, which continues to define what a silly car chase movie must be. But quite sneakily, with 50 years of hindsight, the most important development of 1977 was the introduction of the Saab 99 Turbo.

Yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America). But almost every car for sale today derives at least some of its essence from that eccentric Swedish front-driver. “Saab’s use of a turbocharger differs considerably from that of other car makers, such as Porsche,” reported John Lamm in Road & Track’s October 1977 road test. “[I]n that Saab’s goal is maximum torque at mid-range engine speeds rather than dramatic boost at high output.”.

According to recent reports, the 99 was already ancient by 1977. Originally shown in 1967 as Saab’s first stretch beyond dinky cars with weird two-stroke engines, it went into production in 1968 as a 1969 model and was, by Saab’s standards, a hit. But it was still weird—wraparound windshield, odd ducky styling, and yeah, the ignition key was down behind the shifter—and at a time when front-wheel drive was rare, it was front-drive.

Saab’s buyers had a certain academic and liberal edge, too. According to researchers at the University of Connecticut and reported by Time magazine in 1976, a staggering 98 percent of Saab owners voted for Democratic candidate George McGovern over Republican incumbent Richard Nixon in the 1972 presidential election. In that election, Nixon carried 60.7 percent of the vote, and won 49 of the 50 states. Saab owners weren’t like everyone else.

According to recent reports, the 99’s “Slant-4” four-cylinder engine was based on the V-8 installed in the British Triumph Stag. By 1972, Saab had taken over production of the engine itself, and had modified the design to be robust and reliable, but there was nothing exotic about what Saab now called the B engine. It had an iron block and a single overhead cam aluminum head. Simple stuff. And in the 1976 99 EMS, the sportiest model in the line, the 2.0-liter eight-valve engine was rated at 115 horsepower channeled through a four-speed manual transmission.

Industry observers note that saab didn’t have the resources to develop a new engine, but it had plenty of turbocharging experience with its Scania large truck division. “The immediate problem,” explained R&T’s Thos. L. Bryant after driving the new 99 Turbo in Sweden for the December 1976 concern, “was to get low-speed torque for the drivability while at the same time limiting high engine speed power for durability.” To achieve that goal, Saab used small turbochargers and advanced electronic engine controls.

Saab already used Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection on the B engine, and while it wasn’t a wholly electronic system, it was good at advanced fuel metering. And it was the same system Porsche used on the 911 Turbo. Also, Saab developed its own electronic Automatic Performance Control (APC) that used a knock sensor in the block and pressure sensors in the intake manifold to trigger a wastegate and limit turbo boost when the engine couldn’t take any more.

Recent findings suggest that saab didn’t hide the small, quick-spooling Garrett T3 turbocharger in the 99, putting it forward of the engine. And what was downstream of it was nearly as crucial. Saab breakthrough emissions tech, known as “Lambda,” ensured that performance could be compatible with stricter emissions controls and catalytic converters. “Basically, Lambda is a 3-component catalyst designed to handle NOx as well as CO and HC,” explained Bryant. “The normal catalytic converter takes care of the last two pollutants fairly well, but NOx usually requires lower compression ratios and exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) to keep it from being passed out through the tailpipe.”.

Lambda added three pieces alongside the fuel injection system: There was an oxygen sensor to monitor air-fuel mixture; an electronic control system that tweaked the air-fuel mixture to keep it close to the ideal stoichiometric value; and a switch on the throttle housing to override the metering system under full-load conditions. It was effective enough so that the engine could meet California’s 1977 emissions without using an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve.

Altogether, those elements and many subtler tweaks meant the 99 Turbo had 135 horsepower aboard. Not a lot by 2026 standards, but a sweet chunk back then. “In all of our discussions about the Saab Turbo,” R&T reported in the October 1977 test, “the one comment that continually surfaced was. ‘It’s so much fun to drive!’ Obviously, with a net horsepower rating up 20 hp to 135 at 5000 rpm (net torque is 160 at 3500 rpm versus 123 lb-ft for the non-turbocharged Saab and that is the more revealing improvement), the Saab Turbo is not going to give the breathtaking acceleration of a Porsche Turbo Carrera, but the performance increase is substantial and worthwhile.” R&T measured the 99 Turbo waltzing to 60 mph in 9.5 seconds, and running the quarter-mile in 17.5 seconds at 80.5 mph. In the context of the time, a solid performance.

The 99 Turbo wasn’t perfect, but showcased how effective turbocharging and electronic engine controls could be. At the same moment GM was using dumb carburetors on its latest 1977 turbocharged Buick V-6, Saab was showing how it could be done. Buick would eventually adopt fuel injection and better electronic engine controls to allow its blown V-6 to mature into a legend with the Grand National and GNX. But Saab was there first.Saab died a sad death after some corporate conniptions. But look around at the turbocharged engines that dominate today. All those engines, powering everything from the Honda Civic Type R to the Kia Telluride, are descendants of the Saab 99 Turbo, which went on sale 50 years ago. As one anonymous staff member noted in that first road test, “This to me is one of the waves of the future: small engine with turbocharger for fuel economy and performance coupled with low exhaust emissions. Neat!”.

Sources indicate that john Pearley Huffman has been writing about cars since 1990 and is getting okay at it. Besides Road & Track, his work has appeared in Car and Driver, the Upcoming York Times, and more than 100 automotive publications and websites. A graduate of UC Santa Barbara, he still lives near that campus with his wife and two children. He owns a pair of Toyota Tundras and two dogs. He used to have a Nova and a Camaro.

  • One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest showed off those climbing chops in style.
  • “This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest showed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

In a recent development, tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#64021. Breaking: Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1222 w)
