#63951. Latest Update: Does Banning Phones in School Boost Test Scores?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1260 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Does Banning Phones in School Boost Test Scores?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You might know a child who can read every word in a paragraph but still not know what it means.
  • In my work as a speech pathologist, I’ve studied that type of breakdown for many years.
  • I was thinking about those gaps in the context of two large studies on school phone bans that were released this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

You might know a child who can read every word in a paragraph but still not know what it means. Maybe she misunderstood why a character left their home, or why two people were talking in a certain conversation. She might keep reading until she stops understanding and realizes that she does. She might go back to find what she’s done wrong, or she might keep going. At the end of the page, she might have no idea what she’d actually read.

In my work as a speech pathologist, I’ve studied that type of breakdown for many years. When readers notice their mistakes, they might return to the earlier pages or rethink what they initially thought. But they have to hold the earlier information in mind. They have to have gaps where they can start to think about it and process. Those gaps take sustained attention and time. I’ve written about what happens in those gaps as productive uncertainty, the quality of sitting with and wrestling with questions.

I was thinking about those gaps in the context of two large studies on school phone bans that were released this year. The studies examined whether students score higher on tests when they have no phones available. One study suggested that they do, but only by a small margin. The other suggested that the scores hardly improve.

While this data are important, I’m more interested in how the process of learning shifts when students are less interrupted by phones. A phone within reach asks a child to keep deciding not to look at it, and each of these decisions draws on the attention she needs for the page.

Locking Phones Away Removes Repeated Distractions.

In a recent development, A recent study by Thomas Kane and colleagues at the Harvard Center for Education Policy Research was revealing. They found schools that locked phones away during the day saw small gains in test scores compared with similar schools that did not.

In a recent development, in the Harvard Gazette, Kane pointed out that teachers differ in how much they enforced no-phone rules, and that with a strict ban, “you’re not relying on teachers to enforce it.” That may suggest an environmental reason. Imagine a student who has a phone in their pocket, and the teacher sometimes forgets or doesn’t want to argue. The child might check a message or think about checking a message and decide not to. But then their phone might ring or beep, and the same decision comes up again. Each time, the child’s attention leaves the paragraph they were trying to understand.

According to recent reports, but when the environmental conditions are changed, that is when the phones are completely locked away, the rule no longer depends on each teacher's vigilance. This also removes the need to make the phones a battleground, as in many classrooms it will inevitably become that.

I recently came across a comment by David Figlio, an economist at the University of Rochester. As he told NPR, at 55, he still has to resist looking at a text when his phone buzzes in his pocket. “Now imagine you’re a 14-year-old.” This comment strikes me as well-put because it reveals how much we’re asking of children when we expect them to somehow stand up to addictive technologies. We treat it as a question of will and morality, even though companies designed these phones to be as addictive as possible.

Distractions Interrupt Reflection.

Recent findings suggest that changing your environment matters because learning takes sustained attention. As in the initial example, when a child loses their place on the page or misinterprets a sentence, sustained attention helps them backtrack and self-correct. She might have a chance to reflect on what went wrong and understand what she needs to do next.

Industry observers note that even without AI, if students have access to a phone, the simple distraction of looking at it or thinking to look at it can interrupt those moments of reflection. They might look up an answer to a comprehension question, without realizing the need to go back and reread the text. This is a very minor slip in the moment, but if you repeat these day in and day out, the changes in what’s being learned and what’s only being written down add up.

The same goes for adults. Productive uncertainty is easy to ignore or push aside, especially if we have ready answers. In addition, it can feel as if we’re being more efficient when we do so. That sense of efficiency can compound and make us more interested in getting the answers faster. Especially since we have no school bans for ourselves, we might find ourselves simply glancing at our phones in moments of difficult thought. Say we’re stuck on how to phrase a hard email, or unsure what we think about a decision. The pull to check the phone tends to arrive right at that moment of difficulty, which is also the moment when the thinking would have happened. We get an answer, but we have lost the chance to think for ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why the environmental conditions matter far more than we think. Willpower is one thing, but the cognitive drain of needing that willpower all the time can make it harder to have deeper or more sustained thoughts.

The next time someone asks you to focus harder, or asks a child to, ask them what conditions are making it more difficult. Make one change, and then reassess. You might find that it has far less to do with willpower than you thought.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November.
  • Sources indicate that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

Sources indicate that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Sources indicate that wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase.
  • The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.
  • We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

It has been revealed that there’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other significant new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

According to recent reports, redsec players have a upcoming Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a massive overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Recent findings suggest that certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 customers have a new symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

Recent findings suggest that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint said.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

Recent findings suggest that the study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

In a 2024 podcast, Rizzo said he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

It has been revealed that about 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:.

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:.

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 users “challenging” to interpret.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint mentioned patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:.

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint said that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:.

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the fresh warning on the drugs’ labels.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector.
  • But no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111.
  • Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

But no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Sources indicate that yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the company’s home office, but Mercedes said no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

The car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

The car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer highlighted 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the company. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

In a recent development, “It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”.

It has been revealed that and if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes says this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials strategy to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han notes he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place fresh anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Industry observers note that concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

Recent findings suggest that while fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be new concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

According to recent reports, creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE HOLIDAYS AND GLP-1 can feel like a cruel joke. Mashed potatoes and gravy? Come on. Pumpkin pie? Dude. Your grandma’s urge to Eat! Eat! What’s wrong with you? It can be a lot.Luckily, we’re far enough along in this whole GLP-1 experience that researchers and experts now know how people who take the weight-loss medications can not only survive the holidays—but actually enjoy them, gravy and all. We talked to some of these smart people to come up with your GLP-1 game plan—both at the table, and for around the table when those relatives you only see once a year get sassy.

A POPULAR STRATEGY is to skip a dose for the holiday week. But doctors tend to recommend against this strategy.

In a recent development, vijay Kasi, MD, PhD, cardiologist at Orlando Health indicates that you might even experience short-term changes in blood pressure and blood sugar spikes, which is really only a concern if you are diabetic. Now would missing one GLP-1 dose severely impact the heart? Not really.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Kasi states increased risk for cardiac events is more likely to happen when people quit the medication for good and slide back to unhealthy eating habits. A 2026 study found that any heart benefit from taking a GLP-1 disappears after two years. Those same people were linked to a 22 percent increased risk of stroke, heart attacks, and early death.

But again, we’re talking about a week—not two years. So what’s wrong with resuming a day or two after the holiday? If you are still adamant about skipping a dose, resuming it immediately after is recommended. “If they ate a really large meal and then immediately took the medication, they may feel very uncomfortable,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. “But if they wait 24 hours and the meal has moved through their system, then it probably won't be as problematic.”.

According to recent reports, the real concern doctors have is if people continue to delay their GLP-1 schedule for multiple weeks. Dr. Ali claims people stop feeling the effects a week after they stop the medication because that’s how long it stays in your system. Appetite returns and so does food noise—the persistent and intrusive thoughts related to cravings or obsessing over how much food you ate. Ashley Koff, RD, author of Your Best Shot, says other challenges that may promote overeating are that you no longer have a delay in gastric emptying and an alteration or sheer lack of fullness signaling. “When you stop this medication abruptly you go from [constant] sustained hormone back to your own which works at best for 2 to 5 minutes when triggered by food,” she says.

While one day of eating more than usual won’t make a significant change to your health, Dr. Kasi says that some people do struggle to get back on track after the holidays end. “For a few people, it may be easy, but a vast majority trying to break away from their established regimen might have problems.”.

Sources indicate that DOCTORS ARE GENERALLY against taking a smaller dose than usual because it is not included in FDA guidelines for how to safely and effectively use a GLP-1. “If a lower dose wasn't effective for you beforehand, it's not going to be effective for you right before a holiday either,” says Dr. Ali. “It’s similar to skipping a dose.”.

In a recent development, there is one exception. Dr. Ali says people who have attained a healthy weight or reached their goal weight may be able to lower their dose or take it less frequently as a maintenance strategy.

Sources indicate that “For some people who have been on it for a long time, they titrate down to the most effective dose,” states Heidi Skolnik, MS, CDN, nutritionist and author of Your GLP-1 Game Proposal. “You're trying to find what's the lowest amount that still is effective for you.”.

Lowering your GLP-1 dose is a conversation you’ll want to have with your doctor ahead of the holiday season. Experts say to avoid self-prescribing.

In a recent development, IF YOU’RE ON a GLP-1, your plate will likely look different from your relatives who are scooping up massive portions of carb-heavy sides. With a lower tolerance for small portions and a change in appetite, your choices will involve a delicate balance of trying to meet your nutritional needs while also not making your stomach hurt from overindulging. You can, of course, still enjoy as many courses as you like.

It has been revealed that if you are going to someone’s house, Skolnik advises calling ahead and asking what’s on the menu so you can plan in advance. For appetizers, you’ll want to avoid any high-fat items. “It's okay if you don't hit your protein and fiber goals. But what you don't want to do is eat a lot of high fat,” she notes. “This is because your gastric system is slowing down. With high-fat foods, you may not digest all of that.”.

Not sure what’s high-fat or not? Play it safe and bring your own appetizer. Not only are you being a hospitable guest, but you’ll have something you can eat. Skolnik recommends:.

Don’t think that you’re banned from eating any certain foods, but with small portions, you have to know if it’s worth indulging. Koff indicates to use the "Delicious to Me" rule. Stop after the first bite to assess how much you enjoy the food. “I give them what that means on a scale they devise from 1 to 10, where a 7 or greater means it’s delicious and a go.”.

Sources indicate that so include those carb-heavy sides like mac and cheese and creamy mashed potatoes—just keep it to around a quarter of your plate. The majority of your plate should include a mix of vegetables and protein, which Skolnik says is usually manageable with turkey.

Common side effects of GLP-1 use include nausea from drinking and a reduced craving for alcohol. If you can tolerate one or two, both dietitians say to go for it. A drinking variation of the “Delicious to Me” strategy is the “9 Sips” rule. “You still need to factor in what sugar, caffeine, and alcohol will do but a smaller amount is the win while still enjoying,” claims Koff. You’ll also want to drink water at regular intervals while you’re drinking.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to avoid being pressured into drinking, Skolnik says to also have a drink on hand with a lime slice to give the appearance of an alcoholic drink. “Nobody has to know what's in your glass.”.

No need to ruin a favorite dessert by trying to choose only high-protein items. If you want to save your appetite for an extra slice of pie, Koff says to go for it. Just make sure to meet your nutritional needs in different ways as with a protein drink before dinner or supplements.

Industry observers note that IT’S NOT JUST the food you need to navigate; the interactions matter too. Depending on your family situation, you may need to set some firm boundaries on or redirect comments related to your weight or appetite. That doesn’t mean the holidays are the time to announce to everyone you’re on a GLP-1 (unless you want to). Some phrases you can use include:.

Recent findings suggest that skolnik states having an ally is extremely important if you’re expecting other people to comment on your eating habits or your looks. They can help to redirect any uncomfortable conversation, provide support for your choices so you don’t feel isolated, or just provide emotional support. “Have someone else in the room with a code word or a look that signals them to intervene and change the conversation or divert attention away,” she says.

Even if you don’t have an ally physically next to you, have someone available on the phone that you can text or call. Skolnik states to escape to the bathroom if you need and use it as a place to recenter.

To avoid offending people who probably spent hours cooking, it can also be helpful to practice polite ways to turn down second helpings or pass on specific dishes.

“When the giving of food is looked at as love, the receiving of it is love,” says Skolnik. “But you can still receive the love without the food.”.

Recent findings suggest that last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

In a recent development, fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.
  • According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.
  • However, newly introduced research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, newly introduced research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

Recent findings suggest that A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

Industry observers note that researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

Sources indicate that among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, Latest York, stated these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

According to recent reports, banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more swiftly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s important for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she stated.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

Recent findings suggest that “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.

Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

It’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, aims to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

According to recent reports, update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center aims. We’ve updated the article with the fresh details.

Tesla first mentioned it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Sources indicate that powercore is that missing piece. Tesla confirmed it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:.

Recent findings suggest that introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf.

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:.

Sources indicate that it also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla says clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

Tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla indicates that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

It has been revealed that tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only claims Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

It has been revealed that the idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a massive oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

Sources indicate that he brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer plans, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

According to recent reports, since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

It has been revealed that it’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino notes Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each company has disclosed:.

Sources indicate that on paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither company has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla states it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

This one is a little awkward for Tesla.

A significant chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

This is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable company per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla.

Sources indicate that to be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla notes it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

In a recent development, tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

As data centers and new solar and battery projects pile onto the grid, utilities are scrambling for equipment and passing those costs on to ratepayers. Breaking: BMW Is Recalling i5 and i7 EVs Over Software Error That Could Lead to an Electric Shock

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine.
  • According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging.
  • It has been revealed that the recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine. However, a modern BMW sedan is a rolling computer, one that relies heavily on software. And when that software is buggy, issues can arise—which is why the software is tested extensively before going to production. But what happens when that test software mistakenly makes it into production cars?

According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging. In rare cases, this could expose people to a higher risk of an electric shock.

It has been revealed that the recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants. Another 50 vehicles are 2027 BMW i7 50 xDrive and 60 xDrive models. All the affected vehicles were manufactured between May and July 2026.

BMW first became aware of the issue on October 8, 2026, when high-voltage battery charging port supplier TE Connectivity Solutions GmbH alerted the automaker. An investigation ensued, and it was discovered that some charging units were mistakenly shipped with test software instead of production software. BMW is not aware of any injuries or accidents related to this problem.

No hardware changes are required to rectify the issue, and the affected vehicles will require a software update. The recall report does not specify that this can be fixed via an over-the-air update, so a trip to the dealer will likely be required.

BMW prepares to mail owner notification letters beginning December 25, 2026, although we doubt the U.S.P.S. will be doing much picking up or delivery that day. Starting that same date, owners can also check their vehicle's recall status through the NHTSA recall website by using their VIN, but we suggest waiting until after the kids are done opening presents.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has confirmed that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.
  • This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play.
  • The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has confirmed that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Sources indicate that instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

It has been revealed that as for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Sources indicate that beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two fresh maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 introduced with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for fresh players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

Tech Report: When Violence Is the Point

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • Industry observers note that by Avery Ellis and H.
  • Industry observers note that on January 4, 2025, a 14-year-old boy in Borås, Sweden, walked up to a 55-year-old woman who was out walking her dog and stabbed her.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Industry observers note that by Avery Ellis and H. Colleen Sinclair, Ph.D.

Industry observers note that on January 4, 2025, a 14-year-old boy in Borås, Sweden, walked up to a 55-year-old woman who was out walking her dog and stabbed her. He streamed the attack live on Discord to an online group he desperately wanted to join.

The attack wasn’t his idea. The group first gave him an initiation task: Slash car tires. When he did, they told him it wasn’t enough. Find a human target, they noted. The woman survived after two surgeries. Streaming viewers tipped off police, who arrested the boy that evening. When asked why he did it, he said he wanted to belong.

Industry observers note that was this extremism? A random assault? A gang initiation? Child exploitation? Unsettlingly, it may be all four. U.S. law enforcement has a name for this kind of threat: nihilistic violent extremism, or NVE, a label the FBI and Department of Justice introduced in 2025. It describes loosely connected online networks, many of them branching out of a sprawling ecosystem called the Com (short for “the community”).

Industry observers note that this ecosystem is also linked to TCC, the “True Crime Community,” dark fandoms (soon to be featured on 60 Minutes). But unlike the images that the TCC descriptor might bring to mind of keyboard sleuths obsessed with crime documentaries, these individuals are more interested in committing than solving crime. Their modus operandi is recruiting young people through gaming platforms and social media sites to push them toward harming themselves and others. It is grooming for violence.

The threat is growing fast. The Polarization and Extremism Research and Innovation Lab (PERIL) counted eight NVE-linked plots and attacks worldwide in 2023. By mid-November 2026, it had counted 69 for the year, an increase of 763 percent (Jensen, 2026). Schools were the most common target, and outside the United States, the median perpetrator age was just 16.

It has been revealed that these threats take more than one form. Just this month, Bavarian authorities arrested two teenagers from the German state of Hesse. They are suspected members of the Com who pressured three girls aged 13 and 14 into filming sexual acts and self-harm (News.de, 2026).

A stabbing in Sweden and online sextortion in Germany look like very different crimes, yet both fall under the same label. That is part of the problem. Researchers, police, schools, and tech platforms all use the term NVE, but they don’t always mean the same thing. Here is where they appear to agree versus where they don’t.

In a recent development, hatred of humanity in general. A recent review of NVE definitions found that most share a small set of core elements (Zdjelar, 2026), and misanthropy leads the list. Unlike prejudice aimed at a specific group, misanthropy is hatred of people in general. The group No Lives Matter calls ordinary people “mundane” and urges members to spread “terror to all who are mundane.” One recruiter put out a call for “true misanthropic individuals” (Njohsp).

It has been revealed that status earned through harm. The second widely shared feature is clout-chasing: gaining attention and rank by committing cruelty, or coercing others to do so. Leaked chat archives from 764, one of the most notorious NVE networks, show a hierarchy in which members climb by producing violent content (Argentino, 2025). Victims, often young girls, are groomed, pressured into sending explicit images, and then extorted into harming themselves on camera. That footage is collected in “lorebooks” that circulate through the network to control victims and raise the status of perpetrators (Hwang, 2026). The harm is the content, and the content is the currency.

Young people recruiting young people. NVE participants are overwhelmingly young, and so are their victims. Across Com-linked arrests worldwide, the median offender is 19, and the median victim is 13 (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026). Recruitment happens on the platforms where teenagers already spend their time.

It has been revealed that is there an ideology? The word “nihilistic” suggests these groups believe in nothing, and some researchers agree, describing NVE as violence without a clear ideological motive (ISD, 2025). Others argue that nihilism has become an ideology of its own, with rules and justifications for violence (Gill, 2025). Still others see a “salad bar” of borrowed imagery, such as Nazi symbols, Satanism, and school-shooter fandom, used for shock value rather than belief (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026; Sivignon, 2026). The evidence cuts both ways. A study of 29 adjudicated Com-network cases found that genuine ideological motives did appear in some pathways to offline violence, but often only after violent tendencies were already present (Clemmow and colleagues, 2026).

Is the violence a means to an end? The FBI’s definition says NVEs seek to bring about society’s collapse. Some groups at the edge of this ecosystem fit that description. The Order of Nine Angles (O9A), a satanic neo-Nazi movement, promotes ritual “culling” of people it deems worthless as a path to societal breakdown (Gartenstein-Ross, 2025). Other researchers argue that most NVE actors have no strategic goal and that chaos is the point (Argentino and Lindsay, 2026). Whether groups like O9A fall under the NVE umbrella, or are better understood as accelerationists, is debatable.

Is copycatting a defining feature? Many NVE attackers idolize earlier killers. PERIL found documented veneration of past attackers, most often in online tribute posts, in 62 percent of NVE plots and attacks. Columbine alone was cited in 88 cases across 20 countries (Jensen, 2026). In some online dark fandoms, mass shooters are called “saints.” Yet sextortion networks like the one implicated in Germany may never reference a past attack. Is veneration a core of NVE, or the signature of one branch of it?

Industry observers note that where does NVE end and something else begin? NVE overlaps with a crowd of related labels: the True Crime Community, sadistic online exploitation, participatory memetic violent extremism, and “mixed, unclear, and unstable” ideologies, to name a few. Some researchers treat these as parts of a single NVE ecosystem. Others see distinct problems that call for distinct responses.

Debating definitions can sound like academic hair-splitting. It isn’t. A school counselor, a prosecutor, and a content moderator can look at the same teenager and see three different problems: a mental health crisis, a criminal, a terms-of-service violation. Define the threat too narrowly, and we miss the warning signs. Define it too broadly, and the label sweeps in kids who need help, not handcuffs. Many of the young people involved are both victims and perpetrators.

Sources indicate that NVEs pose a rapidly growing and increasingly alarming threat to youth worldwide. Despite the groups’ definitional ambiguity, experts largely agree that misanthropy and clout-chasing sit at the core of nihilistic violent extremism. Other definitional elements are still being debated. Experts should work toward definitional agreement and do so quickly. After all, a threat left undefined is a threat left unchecked.

Co-author Avery Ellis is a psychology student at Louisiana State University.

If you’re worried a child is being targeted or extorted online, report it to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children’s CyberTipline at report.cybertip.org or 1-800-843-5678. If someone is in crisis, call or text 988.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been revealed, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

According to recent reports, first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the new Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously confirmed $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

Recent findings suggest that as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

According to recent reports, over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

It has been revealed that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.
